messages.text: Hi, I'm Kenji. I'm an NLP PhD student and I'm trying to move into HCI. So my question is, according to the paper, why did the participants struggle to generalize from the examples? Like, is it because the examples were too few, like a small training set?

messages.short_answer: According to the retrieved passages, the paper does not attribute the struggle mainly to too few examples. It points to participants over-generalizing from single data points and limited experience, plus expectations carried over from human-to-human instruction. Some participants also could not see how examples from one domain applied to their own task.

sections.title: What the paper says about the cause
sections.text: The authors describe two fundamental sources of participants' struggles: over-generalization from limited experience, and a social lens that filtered prompts through expectations from human-human interactions. They report that participants over-generalized from single data points, whether positive or negative, often stopping once a behavior appeared in one conversation.

sections.title: Examples that did not transfer across domains
sections.text: Two participants who searched the web for solutions had difficulty using the examples they found. The authors attribute this partly to not seeing how specific prompt designs translated across domains, and one participant judged an example too far from their goal and did not try it.

sections.title: Your training-set hypothesis
sections.text: The passages describe the problem as participants' tendency to overgeneralize from limited experience, not as the number of examples provided. Whether a larger or smaller set of examples changes behavior is not addressed in these passages, so the training-set framing is your hypothesis rather than the paper's finding.

sections.title: Implications for your user study
sections.text: You could separate two factors in your design: how many examples participants see, and whether they are prompted to test a behavior across several conversations before concluding. Measuring how often participants stop after a single observation would test the over-generalization account directly, and cross-domain examples could be varied to test transfer.

messages.text: Ok, I understand better now, thank you. So the design probe in this paper is like a baseline model, right? Like the participants are the test set and the probe is what we compare the prompts against?

messages.short_answer: Not quite. In this paper, the design probe is a research instrument, not a baseline model. BotDesigner is a no-code prompt design tool that the authors built so they could watch how non-experts intuitively approach prompt design. The participants are not a test set, and the passages do not describe comparing their prompts against the probe.

sections.title: What the probe is for
sections.text: The authors say a hands-on tool gives deeper insight than interviews about hypothetical scenarios, and that an open-ended design lets them observe participants' intuitive behaviors and thought processes. The probe is therefore a way to elicit and study behaviour, and the study's aim is to understand how non-experts approach designing robust prompts and where they struggle.

sections.title: Why the baseline/test-set analogy does not fit
sections.text: A baseline model and a test set are used to measure performance on a fixed task. Here, the probe sets up a task in which people's behaviour is observed and interpreted qualitatively, with the authors' findings about over-generalization and human-human expectations emerging from that observation. The passages describe no benchmark or comparison of prompts against the probe.

sections.title: What this suggests for your user study
sections.text: If you use a probe-like tool, it may be better to treat it as an instrument that shapes and reveals users' prompting behaviour, not as a reference system. The paper also notes that the sample is small, skewed toward STEM professionals and students, and not representative, so you would need to think about how your own participant sampling and any comparisons would be designed. You would need to decide yourself whether a probe fits your research questions.

sources.text: We chose to create a design probe because the robustness of prompt strategies is highly dependent on specifc conversational contexts, as is users’ ability to create prompts and debug. Enabling people to engage in designing LLM-and-prompt-based chatbots hands-on offers deeper insights than conducting interviews about hypothetical scenarios alone. We chose to purpose-build a prompt design tool because existing tools focus on enabling non-experts to experiment with various prompting strategies rather than crafting robust and generalizable prompts. 3.1 Designing a No-Code Prompt Design Tool as Probe Design Goals. We have two goals in designing BotDesigner: First, to enable end-users, without any prompt design experience or even programming or ML experience, to (i) create a chatbot using prompts, without code, and (ii) systematically evaluate their prompts. Second, to allow end-users to engage in this process in a fexible, open-ended way, allowing us to observe their intuitive behaviors and thought processes.
quotes: Enabling people to engage in designing LLM-and-prompt-based chatbots hands-on offers deeper insights than conducting interviews about hypothetical scenarios alone.

sources.text: 3 METHOD: DESIGN PROBE In this work, we aim to understand how non-experts intuitively approach designing robust prompts, and whether and how they struggle in doing so. We want to dive deep into what those struggles reveal about people’s assumptions and understanding of promptbased systems in order to inform how end-user-facing prompt design tools might best support their users. We chose to investigate these questions in the context of designing instructional chatbots—chatbots that walk users through an activity (e.g., cooking a recipe, fxing a wif connection) while answering user questions and engaging in social conversation as needed. Chatbot tasks are sufciently open-ended that they open the door to a wide variety of types of problems and prompt-based solution approaches. Instructional chatbots represent a common chatbot use case (e.g., customer service bots), and their constituent tasks are some of the tasks that GPT-3 peforms more efectively out-of-the-box.
quotes: In this work, we aim to understand how non-experts intuitively approach designing robust prompts, and whether and how they struggle in doing so.

sources.text: Two of the authors then compared these approaches across participants and categorized their struggles using afnity diagrams [34] and by creating a service blueprint [5] that documents the specifc approaches individual participants attempt. We chose these methods from HCI and the feld of service design because our focus is on discovering opportunities created by a new technology, rather than understanding how an existing set of users engages in established work practices—a context in which a grounded theory approach would be more conventional. 4 USER STUDY FINDINGS We found the following: (1) Using BotDesigner, all participants were able to engage in ad hoc opportunistic iteration on prompts, with local testing of prompt changes. Two out of our ten participants required assistance in order to begin this process, but could then iterate on their own. (2) Participants’ struggles with generating prompts, evaluating prompt efectiveness, and explaining prompt efects, primarily stemmed from (a) over-generalization from single observations of success and failure of prompt changes; and (b) models of system behavior rooted in human-human interactions.

messages.short_answer: The paper reports ten participants, analysed qualitatively from think-aloud videos through exploratory analysis and affinity diagramming by two authors. The retrieved passages do not describe inter-coder agreement, codebook development or saturation checks, so the reliability of the categorization is unverified.

sections.title: Implications for your user study
sections.text: If your goal is to discover over-generalization patterns among non-experts, a qualitative design similar to this one may suit your question, but you would need to decide the sample size based on that aim. If you want claims about how common these patterns are, you would need a larger or more diverse sample, a clearly documented coding procedure, and reported inter-rater reliability. The final choice of method is yours to make.

sources.text: Using this tool as a design probe, we observed how 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience executed a chatbot design task using BotDesigner, to explore a few diferent pieces of this larger question. Our fndings suggest that, while end-users can explore prompt designs opportunistically, they struggle to make robust, systematic progress. Their struggles echo many well-known struggles observed in end-user programming systems (EUPS) and non-expect users of interactive machine learning (iML) systems. Additional barriers to efective prompt design stem from limited conceptions of LLMs’ prompt understanding and execution abilities and their understandable inclinations to design prompts that resemble human-to-human instructions. We discuss these observations’ implications for designing efective end-user-facing LLM-based design tools, implications for education that improves LLM-andprompt literacy among programmers and the general public, and opportunities for further research. This paper makes three contributions.

sources.text: In this paper, we use chatbots as an example domain to explore the interactions between end user designers and prompt-based systems backed by LLMs (as BotDesigner is). A few additional limitations of our study bear exploration, and point to future studies. First, the reliance on a relatively small pool of likely “early adopters” drawn from academia may skew the observed phenomena towards a specifc set of analogies and preconceived notions around technology and its capabilities. We claim neither that our observations are universal of all end users, nor that they are a complete description of all common misconceptions or behaviors of end-users working with LLM-backed systems. Additionally, the time we gave participants to engage in prompt design was relatively limited, and it is likely that, given enough time and motivation, end users would advance quite quickly in developing better mental models and more efective strategies.

My verdict: Need more evidence
My rationale: I think the probe and think-aloud design are interesting, but the study is only 10 people, mostly STEM students and professionals, and the coding was not checked for reliability, so I cannot yet trust the over-generalization finding for my non-expert users. retrieved.text: Using this tool as a design probe, we observed how 10 participants without substantial prompt design experience executed a chatbot design task using BotDesigner, to explore a few diferent pieces of this larger question. Our fndings suggest that, while end-users can explore prompt designs opportunistically, they struggle to make robust, systematic progress. Their struggles echo many well-known struggles observed in end-user programming systems (EUPS) and non-expect users of interactive machine learning (iML) systems. Additional barriers to efective prompt design stem from limited conceptions of LLMs’ prompt understanding and execution abilities and their understandable inclinations to design prompts that resemble human-to-human instructions. We discuss these observations’ implications for designing efective end-user-facing LLM-based design tools, implications for education that improves LLM-andprompt literacy among programmers and the general public, and opportunities for further research. This paper makes three contributions.

We chose to create a design probe because the robustness of prompt strategies is highly dependent on specifc conversational contexts, as is users’ ability to create prompts and debug. Enabling people to engage in designing LLM-and-prompt-based chatbots hands-on offers deeper insights than conducting interviews about hypothetical scenarios alone. We chose to purpose-build a prompt design tool because existing tools focus on enabling non-experts to experiment with various prompting strategies rather than crafting robust and generalizable prompts. 3.1 Designing a No-Code Prompt Design Tool as Probe Design Goals. We have two goals in designing BotDesigner: First, to enable end-users, without any prompt design experience or even programming or ML experience, to (i) create a chatbot using prompts, without code, and (ii) systematically evaluate their prompts. Second, to allow end-users to engage in this process in a fexible, open-ended way, allowing us to observe their intuitive behaviors and thought processes.

Ultimately, our probe participants explored prompt designs opportunistically, not systematically, and struggled in ways echoing end-user programming systems and interactive machine learning systems. Expectations stemming from human-to-human instructional experiences, and a tendency to overgeneralize, were barriers to efective prompt design. This excitement around LLMs and prompting is propelling a rapidly growing set of LLM-powered applications [23] and prompt design tools [3, 20, 32]. Yet despite widespread excitement, surprisingly little is known about how non-experts intuitively approach designing prompts with LLM-and-prompt-based tools, and how efective they are in doing so. While prompting LLMs can appear efortless, designing efective prompting strategies requires identifying the contexts in which these LLMs’ errors arise, devising prompting strategies to overcome them, and systematically assessing those strategies’ efectiveness. These tasks fall on so-called “prompt engineers”— the designers, domain experts, and any other end-user or professional attempting to improve an LLM’s output—and are challenging tasks even for LLM experts, as well as topics of ongoing research in Natural Language Processing (NLP) [7, 30, 42]. Prompt design tools to date have focused on supporting professional programmers [45] and NLP practitioners [42], rather than non-AI experts, non-programmers, and other potential end-users of these systems.

persona_text:
# Persona: Kenji

**Who.** Kenji is a Japanese PhD student in natural language processing (field A) who wants to move into
human-computer interaction (field B) and run user studies, but knows little HCI methodology. He writes
fluent but imperfect English and occasionally asks for a key term to be explained in Japanese.

**What he wants.** To learn how HCI studies people and to judge which of its methods he could borrow for his
project on how non-experts write prompts for LLM-based tools. Reading goal: *Explore potential use in my
research*.

**How he behaves.**
- Writes in English with small grammar mistakes. Interface language: English.
- Is precise about NLP terms but maps HCI concepts onto NLP ones ("so the participants are like the test
  set?", "is the design probe a kind of baseline model?"). Some of these analogies are wrong.
- Changes focus mid-conversation, e.g. from the findings to how the study was run.
- Asks about the strength of the evidence (number of participants, how the data were coded or analysed).
- Checks the sources often.
- Asks for a critical review of whether a method fits his project; his own verdict sometimes differs from
  PaperLens's suggestion.

**Paper.** Why Johnny Can't Prompt: How Non-AI Experts Try (and Fail) to Design LLM Prompts.
